title: Empty hopes and the philosophers
source_text: Ἐπεὶ δὲ καὶ κούφαις ἐλπίσι φησὶν ὑπάγεσθαι τοὺς χριστιανίζοντας ὁ Κέλσος, φήσομεν πρὸς αὐτὸν ἐγκαλοῦντα τῷ περὶ τῆς μακαρίας ζωῆς λόγῳ καὶ τῷ περὶ τῆς πρὸς τὸ θεῖον κοινωνίας ὅτι ὅσον ἐπὶ σοὶ, ὦ οὗτος, κούφαις ὑπάγονται ἐλπίσι καὶ οἱ τὸν Πυθαγόρου καὶ Πλάτωνος παραδεξάμενοι περὶ ψυχῆς λόγον, πεφυκυίας ἀναβαίνειν ἐπὶ τὴν ἁψῖδα τοῦ οὐρανοῦ καὶ ἐν τῷ ὑπερουρανίῳ τόπῳ θεωρεῖν τὰ τῶν εὐδαιμόνων θεατῶν θεάματα. κατὰ σὲ δὲ. ὦ Κέλσε, καὶ οἱ παραδεξάμενοι τὴν τῆς ψυχῆς ἐπιδιαμονὴν καὶ βιοῦντες, ὥσθ᾿ ἥρωες γενέσθαι καὶ μετὰ θεῶν ἕξειν τὰς διατριβὰς, κούφαις ἐλπίσιν ὑπάγονται. τάχα δὲ καὶ οἱ πεισθέντες περὶ τοῦ „θύραθεν“ νοῦ ὡς (ἀ) θανάτου, καὶ νοῦ διεξαγωγὴν ἕξοντος. κούφαις ἂν ὑπάγεσθαι λέγοιντο ὑπὸ Κέλσου ἐλπίσιν. ἀγωνισάσθω οὖν μηκέτι κρύπτων τὴν ἑαυτοῦ αἵρεσιν ἀλλ᾿ ὁμολογῶν Ἐπικούρειος εἶναι πρὸς τὰ παρ᾿ Ἕλλησι καὶ βαρβάροις οὐκ εὐκαταφρονήτως λεγόμενα περὶ τῆς ἀθανασίας τῆς ψυχῆς ἢ τῆς ἐπιδιαμονῆς αὐτῆς ἢ τῆς τοῦ νοῦ ἀθανασίας, καὶ παραδεικνύτω ταῦτα μὲν εἶναι λόγους, κούφαις ἐλπίσιν ἀπατῶντας τοὺς συγκατατιθεμένους αὐτοῖς. τοὺς δὲ τῆς ἑαυτοῦ φιλοσοφίας καθαροὺς εἶναι κούφων ἐλπίδων καὶ ἤτοι προσάγοντας ἐλπίσιν ἀγαθαῖς ἢ. ὅπερ μᾶλλον ἀκόλουθόν ἐστιν αὐτῷ, οὐδεμίαν ἐμποιοῦντας ἐλπίδα διὰ τὴν τῆς ψυχῆς εὐθέως παντελῆ φθοράν. εἰ μὴ ἄρα Κέλσος καὶ οἱ Ἐπικούρειοι οὐ φήσουσι κούφην εἶναι ἐλπίδα τὴν περὶ τοῦ τέλους αὐτῶν τῆς ἡδονῆς, ἥτις κατ᾿ αὐτούς ἐστι τὸ ἀγαθὸν, τὸ τῆς σαρκὸς εὐσταθὲς κατάστημα καὶ τὸ περὶ ταύτης πιστὸν Ἐπικούρῳ ἔλπισμα.
pass_a_gloss: Since Celsus says also that those becoming Christians (χριστιανίζοντες) are led on by empty hopes, we shall say to him, accusing (ἐγκαλέω) the doctrine about the blessed life (μακαρία ζωή) and about fellowship (κοινωνία) with the divine, that as far as concerns you (ὅσον ἐπὶ σοί), O man (ὦ οὗτος), those too are led on by empty hopes who accepted (παραδέχομαι) the doctrine of Pythagoras and Plato about the soul (ψυχή), being of a nature (πέφυκε) to ascend to the vault (ἁψίς) of heaven and in the place above heaven (ὑπερουράνιος τόπος) to behold (θεωρέω) the sights (θεάματα) of the blessed spectators (εὐδαίμονες θεαταί). According to you, O Celsus, those too who accepted the survival (ἐπιδιαμονή) of the soul and living so as to become heroes (ἥρωες) and to have their dwelling (διατριβαί) with gods, are led on by empty hopes. Perhaps also those persuaded about the mind 'from outside' (θύραθεν νοῦς) as immortal ((ἀ)θάνατος) and as going to have a continuance (διεξαγωγή) of mind, might be said by Celsus to be led on by empty hopes. Let him contend (ἀγωνίζομαι) then, no longer hiding his own school (αἵρεσις) but confessing (ὁμολογέω) he is Epicurean, against the things said not contemptibly (οὐκ εὐκαταφρονήτως) among Greeks and barbarians about immortality (ἀθανασία) of the soul or its survival or immortality of the mind, and let him demonstrate (παραδείκνυμι) that these are arguments deceiving (ἀπατάω) with empty hopes those assenting (συγκατατίθεμαι) to them, but those of his own philosophy are pure (καθαροί) of empty hopes and either bring to good hopes or, what is more consistent (ἀκόλουθον) for him, produce no hope through the immediate complete destruction (εὐθέως παντελὴς φθορά) of the soul. Unless Celsus and the Epicureans will not say it is an empty hope, the one about their end (τέλος), pleasure, which according to them is the good, the stable condition of the flesh (τὸ τῆς σαρκὸς εὐσταθὲς κατάστημα) and the trustworthy expectation (πιστὸν ἔλπισμα) about this, to Epicurus.
pass_b_english: Celsus also says that those who become Christians are led on by empty hopes. Since he thus finds fault with the doctrine of the blessed life and of fellowship with the divine, we shall say to him: By your reasoning, sir, those also who have accepted the teaching of Pythagoras and Plato about the soul are led on by empty hopes, the teaching that the soul is by nature able to rise to the vault of heaven and, in the place above the heavens, to behold the sights that the blessed spectators see (Plato, Phaedrus 247b–c). By your account, Celsus, those too who have accepted that the soul survives, and who live so as to become heroes and to spend their days with the gods, are led on by empty hopes. And perhaps those persuaded that the mind which comes “from outside” (Aristotle, Generation of Animals 736b) is immortal, and will continue its life as mind, might also be said by Celsus to be led on by empty hopes.

Let him, then, no longer hide his own school, but confess that he is an Epicurean, and do battle against what Greeks and barbarians have said, in terms far from contemptible, about the immortality of the soul, or its survival, or the immortality of the mind. Let him show that these are arguments that deceive with empty hopes those who assent to them, while the arguments of his own philosophy are free of empty hopes, and either lead to good hopes or, what better fits his position, instil no hope at all, since the soul is at once utterly destroyed. Unless, indeed, Celsus and the Epicureans will deny that their own hope is empty, the hope about their end, pleasure, which on their view is the good: “the stable condition of the flesh,” and the expectation of it which Epicurus holds sure (Epicurus, fragment 68 Usener).

choices.choice: Copy-text: staged source_3.json section 80 (Koetschau 3.80). '(ἀ)θανάτου' is Koetschau's supplement (immortal), read as printed. Classical sources: the soul's ascent to the 'vault of heaven' and the 'place above the heavens' with its blessed sights is Plato, Phaedrus 247b–c (ἁψίς, ὑπερουράνιος τόπος); the mind 'from outside' (θύραθεν, in quotation marks in the edition) is Aristotle, Generation of Animals 2.3, 736b27–28; 'τὸ τῆς σαρκὸς εὐσταθὲς κατάστημα καὶ τὸ περὶ ταύτης πιστὸν ἔλπισμα' is Epicurus fragment 68 Usener (preserved in Plutarch, Non posse 1089d). The dative 'Ἐπικούρῳ' is taken as 'in Epicurus's view' ('which Epicurus holds sure'). Heroes living 'with the gods': lowercase, a pagan belief Origen reports. 'ὦ οὗτος' rendered 'sir'. 'νοῦ διεξαγωγὴν ἕξοντος' rendered 'will continue its life as mind'. No Scripture quotation or clear allusion.
'As far as you are concerned, sir' changed to 'By your reasoning, sir' (ὅσον ἐπὶ σοί = on your argument; the English idiom could read as 'for all you care')
'and will go on living' changed to 'and will continue its life as mind' (νοῦ διεξαγωγὴν ἕξοντος names the mind's own mode of life, which the draft dropped)
'what has been said, in no way contemptibly, among Greeks and barbarians' changed to 'what Greeks and barbarians have said, in terms far from contemptible' (removes a calque of οὐκ εὐκαταφρονήτως)
Checked classical sources: Phaedrus 247b–c (ἁψίς, ὑπερουράνιος τόπος), Generation of Animals 736b (θύραθεν νοῦς), Epicurus fr. 68 Usener (εὐσταθὲς σαρκὸς κατάστημα ... πιστὸν ἔλπισμα); all correct
Checked 'εἰ μὴ ἄρα ... οὐ φήσουσι' irony kept ('Unless, indeed, ... will deny that their own hope is empty')
